value: did not respond to predator odour (no response to fox or cat urine on dowels at foraging stations)

source.authors: Emma E. Spencer, Mathew S. Crowther, Christopher R. Dickman
source.title: Risky Business: Do Native Rodents Use Habitat and Odor Cues to Manage Predation Risk in Australian Deserts?

method: field experiment: paired food bowls (open sand vs shrub or spinifex) at foraging stations with predator-urine dowels versus untreated control dowels; bowl visits, giving-up density and movement tracks
conditions: Wild spinifex hopping-mouse at Ethabuka Reserve, Simpson Desert, Australia; two field experiments run in sequence at night under a new moon; no captive animals. Experiment 1: fox urine versus no urine, 56 foraging stations at three sites, 3 nights of odour after 3 nights of pre-baiting. Experiment 2: fox urine, cat urine or no urine, 32 stations at two sites, 5 nights of odour after 7 nights of pre-baiting. Odour treatments alternated between stations; randomisation not described; control dowels untreated, no pungency control. Individuals were identified from footprints each morning and the number of individual N. alexis is not reported (152 tracks followed in Experiment 1, 319 in Experiment 2). Mean giving-up density was 18.6 +/- 0.1 SE (n = 175) and 18.1 +/- 0.1 SE (n = 279) peanut quarters left of 20, invariant across odour treatments; odour appeared in no Experiment 2 movement model and in one Experiment 1 movement model with standard error larger than its estimate; the text gives no F or P values for odour (Table 1 not read). The only significant foraging effect reported was habitat: in Experiment 2 mice visited open microhabitats more than sheltered ones (Z = 1.77, P = 0.048). Methods do not say whether other rodent species visited the stations; only N. alexis is reported. The null concerns odour on a dowel next to food, so it does not show the mice cannot detect the urine.
quote: Rodents did not respond to predator odor, perhaps reflecting the inconsistent selection pressure that is imposed on prey species in the desert environment due to the transience of predator-presence.
note: Whole abstract sentence read in two abutting pieces ('...imposed on prey' | ' species in the desert environment due to the transience of predator-presence.'), end verified. value: bycatch of green sea turtles 59.5% lower in gillnets lit with green LEDs than in unlit control nets
units: categorical (percent reduction in bycatch per unit effort, illuminated vs control net)

source.authors: Dwi Ariyoga Gautama, Hendro Susanto, Mochammad Riyanto, Ronny I. Wahju, Michael Osmond, John H. Wang
source.title: Reducing sea turtle bycatch with net illumination in an Indonesian small-scale coastal gillnet fishery

method: paired field experiment in a commercial fishery: illuminated versus unlit control gillnets fished on the same nights; Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test
conditions: Wild green turtles caught as bycatch off Paloh, West Kalimantan, Indonesia, and released alive; April 2014 to June 2017. 70 pairs of control and illuminated nets (140 nets), fished the same night 1 to 2 km apart. Lights were constant (non-flashing) green LEDs, peak 500 nm, every 10 m on the floatline; light intensity not reported; whether net assignment or side was randomised is not stated. Green turtles: 14 in control nets and 6 in illuminated nets, Wilcoxon p = 0.039 (test statistic not reported). Other species in the same experiment had very small counts: olive ridley 7 vs 1 and hawksbill 3 vs 2 (all turtles 24 vs 9; multi-species reduction 61.4% per the abstract, 60.7% in the Discussion). Catch per unit effort of total catch and target species remained similar between treatments (total marketable catch p = 0.370, target catch p = 0.096, non-target catch p = 0.655). The experiment compares nets, not animals: an effect of the lights on turtles is inferred by the authors, and the study cannot separate visual avoidance from other responses to the lit net.
quote: Results indicated that net illumination significantly reduced multi-species sea turtle bycatch by 61.4% and specifically green sea turtles (Chelonia mydas) by 59.5%, while the CPUE of total catch and target species remained similar.
note: Whole abstract sentence read in three abutting pieces, end verified. Eyed animal responding to light, so filed under behaviour_vision. value: no significant reduction in the proportion of sharks interacting with a bait while a commercial electric anklet deterrent was active
units: categorical (null result; proportion interacting with bait, active vs inactive device)

source.authors: Channing A. Egeberg, Ryan M. Kempster, Nathan S. Hart, Laura Ryan, Lucille Chapuis, Caroline C. Kerr, Carl Schmidt, Enrico Gennari, Kara E. Yopak, Shaun P. Collin
source.title: Not all electric shark deterrents are made equal: Effects of a commercial electric anklet deterrent on white shark behaviour

method: field experiment with stereo-video rigs: baited target with an active versus an inactive (visually identical, uncharged) electric anklet deterrent (Electronic Shark Defense System)
conditions: Free-ranging wild white sharks (estimated 2 to 4 m) at Seal Island, Mossel Bay, South Africa, July 2014. 395 encounters (238 control, 157 active) from 44 individual sharks, 51 h of footage; 17 control and 17 active deployments of 90 min each. Bait: a PVC canister with about 0.5 kg of sardines and fish heads suspended 1 m in front of the cameras, so the sharks also had chemical and visual cues, and the test measures the device against a bait rather than isolating the electric sense. Four rigs deployed at once at sites at least 300 m apart and rotated among sites; starting location randomly assigned; treatments spread evenly over locations and time slots. The device discharged at 7.8 Hz for 2.5 s then was inactive for 2.6 s, so many sharks met it in the inactive state. At close proximity (under 15.5 cm) the active device did reduce the number of sharks biting the bait, countered by an increase in other, less aggressive interactions (next abstract sentence). The authors judge the effective range very short and the effect unreliable.
quote: We found that the ESDS had limited meaningful effect on the behaviour of C. carcharias, with no significant reduction in the proportion of sharks interacting with the bait in the presence of the active device.
note: Whole abstract sentence read in three abutting pieces ('...with no significant reduction' | 'in the proportion of sharks interacting with the bait' | 'in the presence of the active device.'), end verified. value: detection rates fell by 30 to 100% at 750 m distance (depending on wind farm) during acoustic deterrent operation, compared with 6 hours before it
units: categorical (percent change in detection-positive minutes at 750 m during acoustic deterrent operation)

source.authors: Julika Voß, Armin Rose, Vladislav Kosarev, Raúl Vílela, Ilse Catharina van Opzeeland, Ansgar Diederichs
source.title: Response of harbor porpoises (Phocoena phocoena) to different types of acoustic harassment devices and subsequent piling during the construction of offshore wind farms

method: passive acoustic monitoring (click detectors, CPODs) of wild porpoises around offshore wind farms, comparing detection-positive minutes before and during operation of an acoustic porpoise deterrent
conditions: Wild harbor porpoises in the German North Sea, March 2018 to April 2019, no captive animals. 207 monopiles; stationary CPODs at 16 stations and mobile CPODs for 187 of the 207 piles; the Methods list five wind-farm project names where the abstract speaks of four wind farms. Deterrent: FaunaGuard Porpoise module, SPL 172 dB re 1 uPa (rms) at 1 m, 60 to 150 kHz; the authors recommend about 25 min and no more than 30 min of operation before piling. Baseline is the phase up to 6 h before the deterrent started, which the authors say is not a true undisturbed reference; phases run in fixed order (pre-deterrent, deterrent, piling, post-piling), no randomisation. At one wind farm (Trianel Windpark Borkum Phase 2) the deterrent malfunctioned during three pilings and a seal scarer was used instead. Eleven pilings above the German noise criterion were excluded. Statistics: Bayesian proportion tests, boosted regression trees (short range), a generalized additive model (long range), AIC selection. The decrease was significant at 750 m and 1,500 m for all wind farms except EnBW Hohe See/Albatross at 750 m and Trianel Windpark Borkum Phase 2 at 1,500 m; reduced detection rates were observed only up to about 2.5 km (abstract). The measure is a displacement or avoidance response to a high-frequency deterrent signal, not a hearing threshold.
quote: Depending on the wind farm, detection rates during APD operation decreased by 30 to 100% at 750 m distance compared to 6 hours before APD operation.
note: Whole abstract sentence read in two abutting pieces ('...decreased by 30 to 100% at 750 m distance' | ' compared to 6 hours before APD operation.'), end verified. value: repelled on first encounter with an active electric deterrent at a mean proximity of 131 cm, corresponding to a mean voltage gradient of 9.7 V/m
units: cm (mean proximity at first encounter) and V/m (mean voltage gradient at that proximity)

source.authors: Ryan M. Kempster, Channing A. Egeberg, Nathan S. Hart, Laura Ryan, Lucille Chapuis, Caroline C. Kerr, Carl Schmidt, Charlie Huveneers, Enrico Gennari, Kara E. Yopak, Jessica J. Meeuwig, Shaun P. Collin
source.title: How Close is too Close? The Effect of a Non-Lethal Electric Shark Deterrent on White Shark Behaviour

method: field experiment with stereo-video rigs: baited target with an active versus an inactive Shark Shield Freedom7 electric deterrent; distance of closest approach measured from stereo footage
conditions: Free-ranging wild white sharks, sub-adults estimated at 2 to 4 m, at Seal Island, Mossel Bay, South Africa. 44 trials (22 control with inactive device, 22 active), 322 encounters (279 control, 43 active) from 41 individual sharks. Bait: a sealed PVC container with about 0.5 kg of sardines and fish heads about 1 m in front of the cameras at about 4 m depth, never removed, so the sharks also had chemical and visual cues and the result measures the device against a bait rather than isolating the electric sense. Four rigs deployed at once at sites at least 300 m apart, rotated randomly among sites through the day, control and active balanced over locations and times. Statistics in Minitab (proportion tests; tests weighted by encounter number or shark ID), mean +/- SE. A Table 1 line (read only through a page summary, not directly) gives mean first-encounter proximity of about 38 cm with the inactive control against 131 cm with the active device, p <= 0.001. The authors report that sharks came somewhat closer on repeat encounters, which they read as some tolerance, and that they found no evidence that the device attracts sharks (from the abstract, paraphrased from a page summary, not quoted). The voltage gradient is the value at the measured proximity, not a separately measured threshold.
quote: Upon their first observed encounter, all C. carcharias were repelled at a mean (± std. error) proximity of 131 (± 10.3) cm, which corresponded to a mean voltage gradient of 9.7 (± 0.9) V/m.
